content:
Fireflies.ai - Meeting Transcript

Title: AcmeAI - Usage Insights deep dive (cost by route/model + exports)
Date: Jan 15, 2026
Start time: 17:05 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes

Attendees:
- Avery Johnson (Redwood Inference)
- Markus Klein (Redwood Inference)
- Chloe Martin (Redwood Inference)
- Jason Lee (AcmeAI)
- Priya Nair (AcmeAI)
- Miguel Santos (AcmeAI)
- Hannah Wu (AcmeAI)

Summary (auto-generated):
AcmeAI asked for a granular cost and usage breakdown by API route and model, with drivers including tokens in/out, cache hit rate, retries, fallbacks, context length distribution, and latency. They emphasized a weekly 'what changed' view for investigating spend deltas and a finance-friendly CSV export with consistent totals vs billing. Security requested RBAC controls for cost visibility and audit logging for exports.

Topics (auto-generated):
- Route + model attribution and normalization (incl. OpenAI-compatible endpoints)
- Cost driver definitions: tokens, cache, retries, fallbacks, streaming overhead
- 'Top cost drivers' and 'What changed?' weekly deltas
- Export: CSV schema, rounding/currency, shareable links, audit logs
- Reconciliation vs invoice totals; tolerances and late-arriving events

Questions (auto-generated):
- How do you bucket model versions/aliases (e.g., llama-3.1-70b vs pinned revision)?
- How are retries counted (client retries vs gateway retries) and charged?
- Can we export by workspace/project and by environment (prod vs staging)?
- What’s the expected freshness/lag of the aggregates?
- Can we hide dollar values for engineers but still show tokens/usage?

Action items (auto-generated):
- Redwood to share sample CSV export + draft schema
- Redwood to confirm OpenAI-compat route normalization rules
- Redwood to outline reconciliation approach vs billing invoice totals
- AcmeAI to send top endpoint list and desired grouping rules

---

Transcript:

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Cool, alright. Thanks everyone for joining. This one’s mostly technical, Markus and Chloe are here. Goal is to go deep on the Usage Insights stuff you asked about—cost by route and model, the “what changed” weekly view, and export for finance.

[00:17] Jason Lee: Yep, that’s right. We’re basically trying to stop guessing. We’ve got, like, three endpoints that drive 80% of spend but we can’t prove it.

[00:26] Priya Nair: And I need something I can hand to finance ops. Like, a CSV, route-level, model-level, with totals that match the invoice. Otherwise it’s dead on arrival.

[00:36] Markus Klein: Makes sense. Before we jump in—quick context check. Are you mostly on the hosted API right now or are you testing dedicated capacity too?

[00:44] Jason Lee: Hosted today. We might do dedicated for prod once we’re confident. We run a mixture: chat completions, embeddings, and a reranker. Most spend is chat.

[00:56] Avery Johnson: Got it. And just to be explicit, the feature we’re discussing is in-console cost and usage insights. We can also do API access to the same aggregated data and export jobs.

[01:08] Hannah Wu: From security perspective, I’m mostly worried about who can see dollar amounts and who can download exports. We need audit logs.

[01:16] Chloe Martin: Yup, that’s in scope for the beta. There’s a role gate for cost views and separate permissions for export. Download events get logged.

[01:25] Miguel Santos: Also our data team wants to ingest the export into Snowflake. CSV is fine, but we need stable columns and consistent rounding.

[01:35] Markus Klein: Okay. Let me share how we think about the core dimensions and the drivers. The base breakdown is by time bucket, workspace/project, route, and model. Optional dimensions include region and deployment mode. Then metrics: requests, input tokens, output tokens, cache hit rate, retries, fallbacks, latency percentiles, and cost.

[01:55] Jason Lee: When you say “route”, is that literally the URL path? Because ours includes IDs. Like /v1/projects/123/agents/abc/run.

[02:04] Chloe Martin: Right, so we normalize it. Think templating. It becomes /v1/projects/{project_id}/agents/{agent_id}/run. Otherwise the cardinality explodes.

[02:16] Jason Lee: Okay, good. But we also use OpenAI compatible endpoints. Like /v1/chat/completions and sometimes /v1/responses. Are those mapped cleanly?

[02:26] Chloe Martin: Mostly yes. There are edge cases where the gateway emits a slightly different path string for streaming variants. We’ve been tightening that up. In the insights UI, you’ll see canonical route names.

[02:38] Markus Klein: And we can group at an “endpoint family” level too—like “Chat Completions” vs “Responses”—if you want a less granular view. But baseline is canonical route.

[02:48] Priya Nair: I actually want the granular. Finance asks “what did we spend on chat completions on Model X”. Then engineering asks “which exact route did it”. So both.

[03:00] Avery Johnson: We’ve seen that pattern. Usually the main table is route+model, and there’s filters to roll up by route only, model only, or route group.

[03:10] Miguel Santos: How do you handle model versions and aliases? Because you’ll see us call “llama-3.1-70b”, but we sometimes pin a revision or use an alias like “prod-chat”.

[03:21] Markus Klein: Great question. We track “model family” and “model version” as separate fields. Alias is stored too, but we recommend bucketing cost on stable family/version so exports don’t show duplicates.

[03:34] Jason Lee: That’s a big one. We had issues with another vendor where alias and canonical both show up.

[03:40] Chloe Martin: Yeah, and we’ve added de-dupe rules. There’s still some cases if the alias resolves differently over the time range. We can talk about that.

[03:50] Priya Nair: For finance, if a row shows up twice, we’re done.

[03:54] Markus Klein: Understood. The export will include both “model_display_name” and “model_family/version”, so you can choose. And we’ll make sure the default rollup is stable.

[04:06] Hannah Wu: On RBAC: can we let engineers see token counts and request volume but hide $ cost?

[04:12] Chloe Martin: Yes. There’s a workspace setting to hide cost amounts. In that mode, you still see usage metrics like tokens and requests, plus performance stats. Export is also blocked unless you have the export permission.

[04:27] Hannah Wu: And audit log includes what? Like who downloaded and what filters?

[04:32] Chloe Martin: At minimum: actor, workspace, time, export id, and file name. We can include filter hash and time range. We’re debating PII sensitivity there, but generally yes.

[04:47] Avery Johnson: We can follow up with the exact audit event fields. Security asked for that in other accounts too.

[05:00] Jason Lee: Okay, cost drivers. The biggest question we get internally is “why did output tokens spike”. So the weekly ‘what changed’ view—we want to pick a route+model and see week over week deltas.

[05:13] Markus Klein: Yep. The concept: for a selected time range, we compute deltas versus prior period. For weekly mode: this week vs last week. And we decompose the cost delta into drivers: more requests, higher average output tokens, lower cache hit rate, more retries/fallbacks, model mix shift, and longer contexts.

[05:34] Miguel Santos: How do you do context length distribution? Like quantiles?

[05:38] Markus Klein: Exactly. Buckets: 0–1k, 1–4k, 4–8k, 8k+. Or configurable. In the UI it’s usually a small histogram, and in export it’s either omitted or included as a few columns.

[05:53] Priya Nair: I don’t need histograms in finance export. I need totals and drivers in plain numbers.

[06:00] Markus Klein: Right. Finance export: route, model, time bucket (day), requests, input tokens, output tokens, estimated cache savings, retries, fallbacks, and cost. Then “delta vs previous period” is more of a UI thing, but we can include it in a separate export type.

[06:18] Jason Lee: Streaming overhead—what is that? We do streaming for chat.

[06:23] Chloe Martin: It’s mostly: streaming tends to have slightly different accounting on partial responses and connection resets. It’s not “extra tokens”, but you’ll see more aborted requests, and sometimes retries. The insights tries to surface “connection terminated” patterns.

[06:37] Jason Lee: So is that attributed as retries?

[06:41] Markus Klein: We separate “retry_count” and “abort_count”. Retry_count includes explicit retried attempts that successfully completed, and aborts are requests that ended early. The tricky bit is billing—some providers charge partially. For Redwood, we bill on generated tokens, so aborts usually show lower output tokens.

[06:59] Priya Nair: But our invoice is in dollars. If your insights says $10,245 and invoice says $10,310, I’m going to get yelled at.

[07:07] Avery Johnson: 100%. The goal is consistent totals vs billing. There can be timing differences—late-arriving events, or end-of-month cutoffs. We usually state a tolerance and show a freshness timestamp.

[07:21] Miguel Santos: What’s freshness? Like near-real-time?

[07:24] Chloe Martin: Not real-time. Think hourly-ish for aggregates. Some dimensions might be lagged more. We show “Data current as of” and “Possible partial data” banner if we’re behind.

[07:38] Jason Lee: Hourly is fine. We mainly want weekly and monthly reporting.

[07:43] Priya Nair: Monthly close, yeah. Also currency—do you export in USD? and rounding to cents?

[07:50] Markus Klein: USD by default, cost stored as decimal with 4–6 fractional digits internally, export rounds to cents unless you ask otherwise. We can also include “cost_unrounded” as a separate column. But finance typically wants cents.

[08:06] Priya Nair: If it’s rounded per row, totals can drift. I’d rather have unrounded and then round at the very end.

[08:12] Markus Klein: That’s a good point. We can do “cost_usd_micros” integer to avoid drift. Then your BI can sum exactly. We’ve done that elsewhere.

[08:22] Miguel Santos: Yes please. Give me micros.

[08:26] Chloe Martin: Noted.

[08:30] Jason Lee: Talk about fallbacks. We sometimes see Redwood fallback to a variant when capacity is tight. We need to attribute cost to the actual served model, but also see “requested model”.

[08:42] Markus Klein: Yes. We track both “requested_model” and “served_model”. In the breakdown table you can choose which to group by. For cost accounting, we generally attribute to served_model, because that’s what ran.

[08:57] Jason Lee: Perfect. Because otherwise it hides the fallback.

[09:00] Hannah Wu: Does fallback imply cross-region? Because data residency…

[09:04] Avery Johnson: In hosted mode we can set policy to keep within region. Dedicated/private can lock down more. For insights, region is a filter and a dimension.

[09:15] Hannah Wu: Okay.

[09:18] Markus Klein: Also, top cost drivers view. This is more like: “show me the top 10 route+model combinations by spend” and for each one, a short explanation of why it’s high or why it changed.

[09:32] Jason Lee: I want that. Like, if output tokens increased 35% week over week, say that. Don’t make me eyeball charts.

[09:40] Markus Klein: Exactly. We generate explainability strings. They’re heuristic-based, but we’re cautious not to be misleading. It might say: “Spend increased +$2.1k (+18%) mainly due to higher output tokens per request (+22%), and lower cache hit rate (-9 pts).”

[09:59] Miguel Santos: Cache hit rate—what exactly counts as a hit?

[10:02] Chloe Martin: Prefix/KV cache hit. If the request shares a cached prefix, we count those tokens as “cache_hit_tokens” and your billable compute is reduced accordingly. Not all models support the same caching profile, but the metric is consistent.

[10:18] Jason Lee: Can you show cache savings in dollars?

[10:21] Markus Klein: We can estimate “cache_savings_usd” based on the marginal token cost, yes. It’s an estimate, but helpful.

[10:30] Priya Nair: Finance will ask if it’s real or estimated.

[10:33] Markus Klein: We label it as estimate.

[10:36] Avery Johnson: Also we can link from that insight to recommended levers: “increase cacheability”, “reduce max_tokens”, “switch model”, “enable batching”, etc.

[10:46] Jason Lee: We don’t need auto-optimization; links are fine.

[10:51] Markus Klein: Great.

[11:00] Priya Nair: Let’s talk CSV export workflow. We need something where I can run it monthly and upload into our finance system. Ideally scheduled, but I know that’s not in scope.

[11:10] Chloe Martin: Correct, scheduled emails are out of scope right now. Export is on-demand, async. You click export, we generate server-side, then you download via signed URL. Shareable link is possible but gated.

[11:25] Miguel Santos: Async is fine. What about size? We might do 90 days.

[11:29] Chloe Martin: We’ll likely cap interactive queries to 30 days for performance, but exports can go longer. There will still be limits—like max rows or forced aggregation. For example, for 90 days you might need daily buckets instead of hourly.

[11:46] Jason Lee: That’s okay. We don’t need hourly over 90 days.

[11:50] Priya Nair: But totals must match the invoice over that period.

[11:54] Avery Johnson: Understood.

[12:00] Markus Klein: Can we dig into what “match invoice” means for you? Is it exact down to the cent, or within a tolerance?

[12:06] Priya Nair: Exact is ideal. Practically, if we can explain differences and keep it under, like, 0.5%, it might pass. But we’ll get questions.

[12:17] Miguel Santos: If it’s timing, we can handle. Like events late-arriving after month end.

[12:22] Chloe Martin: That’s the usual culprit. We can include a “data_complete_through” timestamp and a “late_event_adjustments” line item in the export.

[12:33] Priya Nair: That would help.

[12:36] Jason Lee: Another driver: retries. Sometimes our client retries on 429s. Are those billed? And do you attribute cost per attempt?

[12:45] Markus Klein: If a request attempt generates tokens, yes, it contributes to cost. For insights, we count attempts separately from logical requests if we can. But at minimum, you’ll see total requests and “retry_count”.

[12:59] Jason Lee: But how do you know it’s a retry vs a brand new request? Our idempotency keys are… inconsistent.

[13:06] Chloe Martin: That’s the hard part. If you pass an idempotency key, we can identify. Otherwise we infer based on gateway request id and upstream patterns, but that’s not perfect. In the UI we’ll likely define retry as “server-side retried attempt” and separately show 429 rate.

[13:26] Jason Lee: Got it. We can add idempotency keys.

[13:29] Markus Klein: That would improve attribution a lot.

[13:33] Hannah Wu: Are idempotency keys stored? Any retention issues?

[13:36] Chloe Martin: We store a hashed form in telemetry for aggregation, not the raw string, depending on your settings. For regulated customers we can strip it.

[13:48] Hannah Wu: Okay, we’ll want the hashed.

[13:52] Avery Johnson: We can align on data retention separately, but for the insights feature the retention aligns with telemetry retention policy.

[14:00] Miguel Santos: Can you break down by project/environment? We have staging and prod.

[14:06] Markus Klein: Yes, if you tag it as project or workspace, and environment is supported as a filter. Some customers do “workspace per env”.

[14:16] Jason Lee: We do workspace per env. So that’s fine.

[14:20] Markus Klein: Great.

[14:22] Jason Lee: I want to understand the UI flow. Like, where in the console is it?

[14:27] Chloe Martin: Under Usage & Cost. There’s a new “Insights” tab. First view: overview chart + top cost drivers table. You can filter by time range and workspace. Clicking a row drills into a route+model detail page: metrics over time, context length distribution, cache, retries, and the “what changed” panel.

[14:48] Priya Nair: Is there a way to export from the top table directly?

[14:52] Chloe Martin: Yes, export button respects current filters. It’s basically “export this view”.

[14:59] Priya Nair: Good.

[15:01] Miguel Santos: For BI ingestion, we’d rather call an API than click.

[15:06] Markus Klein: There’s an export API too. You’d create an export job, poll status, then download.

[15:14] Miguel Santos: Perfect.

[15:16] Jason Lee: Can you show example fields? Like columns.

[15:19] Markus Klein: Off the top of my head (might miss one): time_bucket_start, workspace_id, project_id (if applicable), route_canonical, route_group, requested_model, served_model, model_family, model_version, requests, successful_requests, input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_hit_tokens, cache_miss_tokens, retry_count, fallback_count, p50_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, cost_usd_micros.

[15:44] Priya Nair: That’s good. Add currency column maybe.

[15:47] Markus Klein: Sure.

[15:50] Hannah Wu: Add who generated the export in the file metadata? Or do you only keep that in audit logs.

[15:55] Chloe Martin: We keep in audit logs; we generally don’t embed user identity into file content, but the file name can include export id and date.

[16:05] Hannah Wu: Fine.

[16:08] Jason Lee: “What changed” weekly view. We want it to detect: output tokens per request increased, or model mix changed. How do you handle “model mix” if I’m filtering to a specific route?

[16:20] Markus Klein: If you’re looking at a route, we can show “within this route, model distribution changed”. Or if you’re looking at an overall view, it shows which routes/models moved.

[16:31] Jason Lee: Okay.

[16:33] Miguel Santos: We also want to detect a cache hit rate drop. That’s usually prompt changes.

[16:38] Markus Klein: Exactly. And we can point to “prompt prefix changed” indirectly by showing “unique prefix count” increasing, but that’s optional.

[16:48] Jason Lee: Hmm. Unique prefix count might be sensitive.

[16:51] Hannah Wu: Yeah. Don’t export that by default.

[16:54] Chloe Martin: Agree. That would be an internal metric, probably not exported.

[17:00] Priya Nair: Another thing: We have internal chargeback. We map routes to teams. If route normalization changes, our mapping breaks.

[17:09] Chloe Martin: Good point. Route normalization rules are versioned. We can keep a stable canonical form and publish the template. If we change it, it’s a flagged change.

[17:21] Jason Lee: We’d want to know when that changes.

[17:23] Avery Johnson: We can commit to documenting it and notifying during beta/GA changes.

[17:30] Markus Klein: Also, you can include your own “x-team” tag as a custom dimension. But fully custom dims are out of scope for initial release. So likely you’ll do mapping on your side.

[17:44] Miguel Santos: That’s fine.

[17:46] Jason Lee: Query performance. We tried a prototype in another system and it times out for 30-day range.

[17:52] Chloe Martin: We’ve been optimizing. The query endpoints will have caching and pre-aggregation. But we might still warn for 30 days at very fine granularity. We can encourage “day bucket” for 30 days.

[18:08] Jason Lee: Okay. As long as export works.

[18:11] Markus Klein: Export uses the warehouse more directly, so it’s less constrained by interactive latency, but it still can’t be unbounded.

[18:20] Priya Nair: We’re okay with “your export will be ready in 5 minutes.”

[18:23] Avery Johnson: Great.

[18:26] Hannah Wu: For shareable reports: are you doing link sharing? We prefer not.

[18:31] Chloe Martin: Link sharing is optional and gated. You can disable. For beta, we can leave it off.

[18:38] Hannah Wu: Keep it off.

[18:39] Avery Johnson: Done.

[18:42] Jason Lee: Quick compare: We looked at Bedrock’s cost explorer and OpenAI’s usage page. They don’t show route-level, just model-level. So route-level is the win.

[18:52] Markus Klein: That’s the wedge, yeah.

[18:55] Priya Nair: Also, I need “consistent totals vs billing.” Sorry to repeat.

[18:59] Avery Johnson: No, it’s the main thing.

[19:02] Markus Klein: Let’s talk about the reconciliation. Our approach: billing is computed from metering events. Insights uses aggregated metering events. So conceptually, they should match. Differences happen from rounding, time zone cutoffs, and late events. We can provide a reconciliation report: insight_total vs billed_total with drift and reasons.

[19:28] Miguel Santos: Time zone is big. Our finance closes on PST.

[19:32] Chloe Martin: The API takes a timezone parameter. UI defaults to workspace timezone. That way day boundaries align.

[19:41] Priya Nair: Great.

[19:44] Jason Lee: Another edge: fallback model costs. If you show served_model cost, does it still count toward requested model totals? Like if I filter requested model, do I see fallbacks?

[19:56] Markus Klein: If you filter requested_model=ModelA, you’ll still see served_model=ModelB costs as part of that filtered set. Then you can break down by served_model to see the fallback.

[20:10] Jason Lee: Perfect.

[20:12] Chloe Martin: We also track “fallback_reason” in a limited set of categories. That might be a driver.

[20:18] Jason Lee: Nice.

[20:20] Priya Nair: Can we include “credits” or “discounts” in cost? Or is it pure usage cost.

[20:26] Avery Johnson: The insights is usage cost. Discounts/credits appear on invoice. We can show a note that invoice includes adjustments. Some customers want “effective cost” but that’s phase 2.

[20:40] Priya Nair: Okay, but call it out clearly.

[20:43] Markus Klein: Will do.

[20:46] Miguel Santos: On the export API—authentication. Is it same token as console? And can we restrict it to our finance service account.

[20:54] Chloe Martin: Yes. You can create a service account with export permission, and log its downloads separately.

[21:03] Hannah Wu: That’s required.

[21:05] Chloe Martin: Great.

[21:08] Jason Lee: I’m thinking about the “top cost drivers” explanation copy. Please don’t be too hand-wavey.

[21:14] Markus Klein: Totally. It’ll point to the exact deltas. But we’ll also show the underlying numbers so you can verify.

[21:23] Jason Lee: Good.

[21:24] (crosstalk)

[21:26] Priya Nair: I want to avoid a scenario where engineering says “the console is wrong.” If it’s derived, I want it transparent.

[21:34] Avery Johnson: That’s why we’re including definitions and tooltips. Also we’ll provide docs on how tokens are counted, how cache hits are counted, what retries mean.

[21:45] Miguel Santos: Are you going to expose raw events? Probably not.

[21:48] Chloe Martin: Not in this feature. It’s aggregated.

[21:52] Jason Lee: That’s fine.

[22:00] Markus Klein: Let’s do a quick hypothetical. Suppose /v1/chat/completions on llama-3.1-70b is $40k this week. The drivers might be: output tokens per request went from 600 to 900, requests up 10%, cache hit rate down from 35% to 20%. We’d show those deltas and recommend actions: reduce max_tokens, add stop sequences, cache system prompt, or switch to a smaller model for certain routes.

[22:26] Jason Lee: Yep. That’s exactly what we want.

[22:29] Priya Nair: And I want to export the table and annotate it for QBR.

[22:33] Avery Johnson: Noted.

[22:36] Hannah Wu: Any PII in the insights? Like prompt text?

[22:40] Chloe Martin: No prompt text. Only metrics and normalized route templates. Model names, tokens, counts. If you pass customer ids as path params, those are templated out.

[22:54] Hannah Wu: Okay.

[23:00] Miguel Santos: One more: We sometimes batch requests. Will that show? Because cost per request changes.

[23:06] Markus Klein: We can show effective tokens/request and latency. But explicit batching metadata depends on instrumentation. If it’s internal batching, it might not show as a separate field.

[23:17] Miguel Santos: Got it.

[23:20] Jason Lee: Okay. Timeline? When can we see this?

[23:23] Avery Johnson: We’re targeting a beta cohort soon. For you, we can probably get you in that list. We’ll need to ensure your account has route tags properly instrumented. That’s a prerequisite.

[23:36] Jason Lee: How do we check that?

[23:38] Chloe Martin: We can run a quick data audit on your metering events. If route is missing, we’ll help instrument. Usually it’s already there for standard endpoints.

[23:52] Markus Klein: If you have custom gateway routes, we might need mapping.

[23:56] Jason Lee: We do have a couple custom ones.

[23:58] Markus Klein: Okay, so action item: send us your top routes list.

[24:03] Priya Nair: And for export, please send a sample CSV. I want to validate columns.

[24:08] Markus Klein: Will do.

[24:10] Avery Johnson: Great. We’re at about halfway. Anything else we didn’t hit?

[24:15] Miguel Santos: Just confirm: export totals vs billing. You’ll provide a reconciliation view.

[24:20] Chloe Martin: Yes, plus freshness timestamps.

[24:23] Hannah Wu: And RBAC and audit logs.

[24:25] Chloe Martin: Yes.

[24:27] Jason Lee: And OpenAI compat endpoints route normalization.

[24:30] Chloe Martin: Yes, I’ll confirm specific mapping for /v1/responses and streaming.

[24:37] Avery Johnson: Cool. I propose next steps: Markus sends sample CSV schema and a sample file, Chloe confirms route normalization behaviors, and we schedule a follow-up to look at mock “what changed” cards.

[24:52] Jason Lee: Works.

[24:53] Priya Nair: Works.

[24:55] Hannah Wu: Works, but include me on the audit log details.

[24:58] Avery Johnson: Will do.

[25:00] Markus Klein: Great. I’ll also include notes on cost_usd_micros vs rounding.

[25:06] Priya Nair: Thank you.

[25:10] (The group continues with detailed Q&A on minor fields, time bucket options, and examples of route templates. Some speaker attribution is unclear in the recording.)

[41:22] Speaker 2: Just to confirm, we can filter to a specific workspace and then export only that?

[41:27] Chloe Martin: Yes. Filters apply to export.

[41:30] Speaker 2: And the export job is async, you said.

[41:33] Markus Klein: Yup.

[49:05] Jason Lee: Alright, I think we’re good. Please send the sample CSV and we’ll sanity check. Then we’ll send back routes.

[49:13] Avery Johnson: Perfect. Thanks everyone.

[49:16] Markus Klein: Thanks.

[49:18] Chloe Martin: Thank you.

[49:20] Priya Nair: Thanks.

[49:22] Hannah Wu: Thanks.

---

Notes:
- AcmeAI emphasized route+model granularity, weekly “what changed” insights, and finance-grade CSV exports with reconciliation.
- Security wants cost visibility RBAC, export audit logs, and share-link disabled.
- Data team requested cost_usd_micros to avoid rounding drift and stable columns for Snowflake ingestion.
